item.title: Rightmove launches new agent tool following Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Rightmove has introduced a streamlined rent review feature to its Tenancy Manager platform, helping letting agents adapt to regulatory changes under the Renters’ Reform Act. The new tool enables agents to generate and serve Section 13 rent increase notices directly within existing tenancy records, potentially reducing administrative burdens and improving compliance with rental legislation.

Simplifying rental administration

The update forms part of Rightmove's ongoing efforts to digitise and connect different stages of the lettings process. Agents can now manage rent reviews alongside other tenancy documentation within the same system, rather than maintaining separate processes. This integration could prove particularly valuable as the private rental sector navigates recent regulatory changes affecting tenancy agreements and rent adjustments.

Rightmove reports the rent review functionality was among the most requested improvements from letting professionals. The enhancement builds upon the platform's existing Lead to Keys suite, which already handles property advertising, enquiry management and tenancy progression. By centralising these functions, the system aims to save time for agents while maintaining rigorous compliance standards.

Broader platform enhancements

Alongside the rent review update, Rightmove has implemented several other improvements to its lettings technology:

  • Digital ID verification within Rightmove Referencing, allowing applicants to confirm their identity electronically
  • PEPs and sanctions screening for landlords, tenants and guarantors via Rightmove Plus
  • Further integration between different stages of the tenancy lifecycle

Tarah Lourens, Rightmove's chief technology and operations officer, commented: "The lettings sector continues to adapt to significant changes, and we're committed to helping agents navigate these developments with confidence. Our rent review feature aims to make essential processes more efficient while maintaining service quality for both landlords and tenants."

These technological advancements arrive as letting agents face increasing regulatory complexity and administrative demands. Rightmove's approach focuses on creating a more connected rental experience that could benefit all parties in the private rented sector - from initial property advertising through to ongoing tenancy management.

item.title: New approach could slash property transaction times
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New proposals could revolutionise the UK property market by dramatically speeding up transactions and reducing the number of collapsed sales. Recent analysis by LawtechUK, a Ministry of Justice-backed initiative, suggests that starting legal preparations earlier in the process may help achieve these long-sought improvements.

The case for early legal preparation

Traditionally, the conveyancing process only begins after a buyer is found, creating unnecessary delays. However, LawtechUK's research indicates that initiating legal work when a property is first listed could slash transaction times. Data from 500 test cases showed freehold properties reaching exchange in roughly 30 days, with leaseholds taking about 45 days - significantly quicker than current averages.

The early preparation model also appears to reduce fall-through rates to below 5%, compared to the national average of around 25-30%. This approach aligns with the government's Home Buying and Selling Reform Roadmap, which advocates for more upfront property information and greater use of digital technology throughout the transaction process.

How technology is transforming conveyancing

Several legal technology firms are already pioneering solutions that could make the home-moving process more efficient. These innovations include:

  • Automated due diligence checks
  • AI-assisted conveyancing tools
  • Real-time communication platforms
  • Shared transaction data systems

One such system, Conveyo, demonstrates how early legal instruction works in practice. When an estate agent lists a property, the seller immediately instructs a solicitor to gather all necessary legal documents. This preparation happens concurrently with the marketing period, rather than waiting for an offer to be accepted.

The potential benefits extend beyond speed. YouGov research commissioned by LawtechUK reveals that 27% of homebuyers find conveyancing causes prolonged stress, while 9% have considered abandoning purchases due to the anxiety involved. More efficient processes could help alleviate these pain points.

The road ahead for property reforms

While some changes will require legislation, many improvements can be implemented using existing technologies. The government's roadmap includes proposals for standardised sales packs prepared before marketing begins, along with standards for AI use in conveyancing.

For homeowners considering selling, these developments could mean less time between accepting an offer and completion. Estate agents may also benefit from reduced fall-through rates, allowing them to focus on progressing firm sales rather than rescuing collapsing chains.

As the property market continues to evolve, these technological and procedural advances could mark the beginning of a more efficient, less stressful home-moving experience for all parties involved.

item.title: Property TV presenter Kirstie Allsopp airlifted to hospital
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Property presenter Kirstie Allsopp has shared details of a serious accident that occurred during her recent birthday celebrations in Devon. The Channel 4 star, best known for co-presenting Location, Location, Location, was airlifted to hospital after slipping on a muddy path whilst walking back from a family picnic at Welcombe Mouth beach.

Emergency Response and Surgery

Following the fall, Kirstie’s 18-year-old son, Oscar, quickly sought help. Emergency services, including RNLI Bude Lifeboat paramedics and Cornwall Air Ambulance, were dispatched to assist. Kirstie was later transported to Barnstaple Hospital, where she underwent surgery for injuries sustained to her leg.

The presenter shared updates on social media, posting photographs of her bandaged leg and an X-ray taken after the operation. She also posted a picture from the ambulance, showing cuts to her face. Kirstie expressed her gratitude to the hospital staff, describing them as “amazing, kind and caring”. She added that she hoped to return home soon.

Reflection on the Incident

Kirstie described the accident as an unforgettable birthday experience, stating that it was “not a birthday I am going to forget”. The incident occurred during a family celebration, which included a picnic and swim at the picturesque Welcombe Mouth. Despite the ordeal, Kirstie remained positive, focusing on the swift response of the emergency teams and the support of her family.

As one of the UK’s most recognisable property experts, Kirstie’s accident has drawn attention from fans and well-wishers alike. Her openness about the incident has highlighted the importance of safety during outdoor activities, particularly in challenging terrain.

A Familiar Face in Property

Kirstie Allsopp has become a household name through her work on Channel 4’s Location, Location, Location, which she co-presents with Phil Spencer. The show, which has been on air for over two decades, has cemented her reputation as a trusted voice in the property market. Her recent accident serves as a reminder of the unexpected challenges life can bring, even during moments of celebration.

As Kirstie recovers from her injuries, fans will no doubt be eager to see her back on screen, continuing to guide viewers through the complexities of buying and selling homes. In the meantime, her positive outlook and gratitude for the support she received during the incident are a testament to her resilience.

item.title: New rental pricing tool targets costly mistakes under Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A new property technology tool aims to help letting agents and landlords set more accurate rental prices by analysing which homes prospective tenants reject during their property searches. Launched by proptech firm nHabit, the platform comes as agents adapt to stricter pricing rules under the Renters’ (Reform) Act.

How the rental pricing tool works

The innovative platform uses anonymised data from nHabit’s consumer property app, tracking not just properties renters show interest in, but also those they dismiss. By analysing rejection patterns across different postcodes and property types, the tool highlights where asking rents or property features may be deterring potential tenants.

Unlike traditional property portals that primarily track engagement, this system provides insights into rental demand sensitivity. Agents can access breakdowns showing whether rejections relate to price, location, property condition or other factors. The company suggests this could help landlords avoid overpricing properties before listing them on the market.

Changing landscape for rental pricing

The tool’s launch coincides with significant regulatory changes affecting the private rental sector. Since 1 May 2026, landlords and agents have been prohibited from accepting offers above the advertised rent under the Renters’ (Reform) Act. Combined with restrictions on rent increases and the abolition of Section 21 evictions, these changes make accurate initial pricing more crucial than ever.

Steven Charlton, founder of nHabit, commented: “We aim to understand renting like dating apps understand relationships. This level of insight comes from tracking both positive and negative responses to property listings.” The company reports its consumer app has been gaining 150-300 new London users daily since launching in February 2026.

What renters prioritise

Early data from the platform suggests renters consider multiple factors beyond headline rents when choosing properties. Location quality, transport links, property condition and long-term affordability all influence decision-making. The tool allows agents to see how these different elements affect tenant choices in specific areas.

For letting professionals, the potential benefit is clear – identifying unrealistic asking prices before properties struggle to attract interest in an increasingly regulated market. As the rental sector continues to evolve, such data-driven approaches may become more commonplace in helping landlords and agents navigate the changing landscape.

item.title: Property firms face £645m HMRC tax scrutiny
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) has significantly increased its scrutiny of major UK property firms, with potential additional tax liabilities under review reaching £645m for the 2025-26 financial year. This represents a 40% rise from £461m the previous year, according to data obtained by law firm Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner (BCLP). The figures highlight growing tax compliance efforts targeting Britain's largest property companies.

Increased HMRC focus on property sector taxation

The £645m figure relates to HMRC's "tax under consideration" metric - an estimate of maximum potential liabilities before full investigations conclude. These examinations fall under the Large Business Directorate, which oversees taxation for approximately 2,000 of the UK's biggest enterprises, including major listed property groups.

Industry analysts suggest this sharp increase reflects HMRC's broader compliance expansion. The tax authority recruited over 1,600 compliance officers during 2025-26, with plans to add 5,500 more by 2030. These staffing boosts contributed to HMRC exceeding £50bn in compliance yield for the first time last year.

Property companies might wish to review their tax positions carefully as this enhanced scrutiny continues. The sector's complex transactions and high-value assets often present multiple areas for potential tax disputes, particularly around corporate structures and cross-border arrangements.

Reduced clarity on tax treatment concerns businesses

Alongside increased investigations, BCLP's research reveals HMRC has become less willing to provide pre-transaction tax clarity. Freedom of Information data shows the tax authority rejected 41% of requests for tax treatment confirmation in 2025-26 - the highest refusal rate in five years.

The situation appears particularly challenging for corporation tax queries, where HMRC declined 63% of requests - more than double the previous 25-30% rejection rate. This shift could complicate business planning, as companies may face greater uncertainty when structuring major property transactions.

Tax specialists note that while HMRC's compliance drive aims to protect public finances, the reduced willingness to provide upfront guidance might lead to more disputes. Commercial property investors and developers may need to factor in potential delays when seeking tax certainty for complex deals.

As HMRC continues expanding its compliance operations, the property sector appears set for ongoing tax scrutiny. Businesses may wish to seek professional advice to ensure their tax affairs remain compliant whilst navigating this changing enforcement landscape.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #452
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

September has brought a wave of updates for landlords and tenants alike, with shifts in rental practices, tenant preferences, and legal proceedings making headlines. From guarantor requests to outdoor space appeal and rent tribunal cases, the property market continues to evolve. Here’s a closer look at the latest developments.

Landlords Increasingly Requesting Guarantors

Recent research suggests that over half of landlords are now asking tenants to provide a guarantor if affordability checks prove challenging. This marks a significant shift from previous practices, where landlords might have requested more than one month’s rent upfront. However, changes under the Renters’ Rights Act have limited this option.

For tenants, this new requirement could influence their property search. Around 51% of renters stated they would look for a cheaper property if asked for a guarantor, while 16% said they might abandon their search altogether. Letting agents have highlighted a lack of awareness among tenants about their options when faced with such requests. For landlords, having a clear and legally sound guarantor agreement is essential to protect their interests.

Outdoor Space Remains a Key Tenant Priority

A survey conducted by CIA Landlords has revealed that rental properties with outdoor space are significantly more appealing to tenants. Of the 72,930 properties surveyed, 36.2% featured gardens, with Edinburgh topping the list at 55.5% and Leeds trailing at just 25.7%. Nearly three-quarters of tenants consider outdoor space an important factor when choosing a rental property.

However, landlords are advised to clearly outline responsibilities for garden maintenance in tenancy agreements to avoid disputes. Ensuring tenants understand their obligations can help maintain the property’s appeal and condition over time.

Rent Tribunal Cases on the Rise

Since the introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act, there has been a notable increase in rent tribunal cases, with tenants now feeling more empowered to challenge rent increases. Data from Hamptons shows a sharp rise in cases, from 44 in July 2025 to 166 in July this year. Monthly averages have also climbed significantly, reaching 129 decisions in June compared to 42 in late April 2026.

Tenants are increasingly turning to tribunals as a cost-effective way to dispute rent hikes. Even if unsuccessful, the process can delay increases for several months, and under current rules, landlords cannot backdate rent adjustments. It is crucial for landlords to provide robust evidence when proposing rent increases, including comparable local lettings, property condition, and amenities. Strict compliance with the statutory Section 13 process is also essential to avoid legal complications.

The rental market continues to adapt to legislative changes and shifting tenant preferences. Whether it’s navigating guarantor requests, catering to outdoor space demand, or addressing rent tribunal challenges, landlords and tenants alike must stay informed to make the most of the evolving landscape.

item.title: Mortgage rate warning threatens autumn housing market recovery
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market could face fresh challenges this autumn as rising wholesale borrowing costs threaten to push mortgage rates higher. Recent turbulence in global bond markets has driven UK government borrowing costs sharply upwards, with implications for fixed-rate mortgage pricing. This development may create headwinds for estate agents and borrowers alike, particularly as the traditionally busier autumn selling season approaches.

What’s driving the pressure on mortgage rates?

Swap rates, which lenders use to price fixed-rate mortgages, have risen significantly in recent weeks. Five-year swap rates climbed above 4.5% this week, reaching their highest level since October 2023, while two-year swaps have also seen sharp increases. These movements are linked to a global bond market sell-off, driven by concerns over inflation, government borrowing, and geopolitical tensions.

UK government borrowing costs have risen particularly sharply, with the yield on 10-year gilts reaching around 5.29%, the highest level since 2008. Meanwhile, 30-year gilt yields climbed above 5.9%, levels not seen since 1998. Whilst gilt yields do not directly determine mortgage pricing, rising swap rates can quickly influence the fixed-rate deals offered by lenders, potentially leading to higher costs for borrowers.

What could this mean for borrowers?

Currently, the average two-year fixed mortgage stands at 5.59%, with the average five-year fix at 5.63%. Experts suggest that if wholesale borrowing costs remain elevated, lenders may begin repricing their mortgage products upwards in the coming days and weeks. This could impact both prospective buyers and homeowners approaching the end of their fixed-rate deals.

Tom Simpson, managing director of homes at Yorkshire Building Society, noted that the impact on mortgage rates could be relatively modest if current market movements persist. He highlighted that swap rates have risen by around 0.1 percentage points over the past week, compared to a more significant increase of 0.5 percentage points during the volatility seen in March. However, other property experts, such as Lucian Cook of Savills, anticipate lenders may increase fixed-rate mortgage costs further in the near term.

Implications for the housing market

For estate agents, another increase in borrowing costs could dampen buyer affordability and confidence, particularly for first-time buyers and those approaching remortgaging. Karen Noye, mortgage expert at Quilter, warned that sustained higher swap rates could put upward pressure on fixed mortgage pricing, creating additional challenges for those entering the market or renewing their deals.

As the autumn selling season unfolds, homeowners and buyers may wish to monitor mortgage rate trends closely. Whilst the situation remains fluid, understanding the factors influencing mortgage costs could help borrowers make more informed decisions during this period of uncertainty.

The coming weeks will be crucial in determining how lenders respond to these market shifts. Borrowers might consider seeking advice from mortgage brokers or financial advisers to navigate the changing landscape and secure the most favourable terms for their circumstances.

item.title: The UK property market is not struggling. So why does it feel like it is?
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent property market figures paint a more optimistic picture than some might expect, with healthy activity levels and a steady flow of sellers and buyers. item.title: Time to hike interest rates, warns Bank of England chief economist
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The Bank of England’s chief economist, Huw Pill, has recently highlighted the need for potential interest rate rises, sparking concerns for mortgage borrowers across the UK. With inflation risks exacerbated by the ongoing Middle East energy crisis, Pill emphasised the importance of tighter monetary policy, questioning the Bank’s current “wait-and-see” stance. His remarks come at a critical juncture for the property market, as rising wholesale borrowing costs could lead to higher fixed mortgage rates, impacting affordability for many homeowners.

Inflation Risks and Monetary Policy

Huw Pill, one of two members of the Bank’s nine-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) who voted for an interest rate increase in July, argued that raising the Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% would send a “clear and unambiguous signal” of the MPC’s commitment to tackling inflation. Speaking at the Edinburgh Chamber of Commerce, Pill warned that economic uncertainties, particularly around energy prices, are likely to persist, making it difficult to predict when inflation pressures might ease. He stated, “Given all this, I am uncomfortable with a ‘wait-and-see’ framing of the MPC’s current decisions over bank rate.”

The chief economist’s comments underscore the delicate balance policymakers face in managing inflation while supporting economic stability. Higher energy prices, driven by geopolitical tensions, have already created upward pressure on inflation, which could further influence interest rate decisions in the coming months. Pill noted that waiting for uncertainties to resolve themselves before acting could delay necessary measures to curb inflation, potentially prolonging economic challenges.

Impact on the Property Market

Rising interest rate expectations have a direct impact on the property market, particularly through their influence on swap rates, which lenders use to price fixed-rate mortgages. Any sustained increase in these rates could lead to higher mortgage costs, placing additional pressure on affordability for borrowers. First-time buyers and homeowners nearing the end of their fixed-rate deals may feel the greatest impact, as they face the prospect of securing new mortgages at potentially higher rates.

The timing of Pill’s remarks is particularly significant as the property market enters its traditionally busier autumn season. Higher mortgage rates could weaken buyer confidence, slowing demand and affecting overall market activity. For homeowners considering remortgaging, it could be worth exploring options sooner rather than later, as lenders may adjust their rates in response to shifting economic conditions.

What Borrowers Might Consider

In light of these developments, borrowers might consider reviewing their current mortgage arrangements and exploring whether locking into a fixed-rate deal could provide stability amid rising costs. Those approaching the end of their fixed-term mortgage may wish to start planning early, as securing a competitive rate before further increases could help mitigate potential financial pressures.

While the Bank of England’s future decisions remain uncertain, Huw Pill’s comments highlight the importance of staying informed about economic trends and their potential impact on mortgage rates. Borrowers seeking clarity on their options may find it beneficial to consult a mortgage adviser or use online comparison tools to assess the best deals available in the current market.

As the UK navigates these economic uncertainties, homeowners and prospective buyers alike will need to remain vigilant, ensuring they are well-prepared for any changes in mortgage rates and broader financial conditions.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Daniel Gale has been promoted to national auctions director at First for Auctions, a subsidiary of Leaders Romans Group (LRG). This move follows the continued expansion of the auction business across the UK. Gale, who previously served as head of auctions, will maintain responsibility for the strategy and performance of the operation while taking on additional duties. These include growing the network of independent estate agency partners and overseeing the auction services across LRG’s residential sales businesses.

A Period of Growth for First for Auctions

Gale’s promotion comes at a time of significant growth for First for Auctions. The business held its largest auction to date in October 2025, featuring a catalogue of 70 lots. Since then, it has been expanding its partnership model, which allows independent estate agents to offer a managed auction service under their own brand. This approach has proven successful, providing agents with a valuable additional route to market while maintaining their client relationships.

Gale’s career in property began in 2005, and he joined Romans, now part of LRG, two years later. He moved into the Auctions and Commercial team in 2010 and was appointed Head of Auctions in 2022. His leadership has been instrumental in the development of First for Auctions into a nationwide online auction operation, as well as the expansion of its independent agent partner network.

Recognition and Future Opportunities

Kevin Shaw, national sales managing director at LRG, praised Gale’s achievements and highlighted the opportunities ahead. “Daniel’s promotion reflects both what he has achieved at First for Auctions and the scale of the opportunity ahead,” Shaw said. “He has developed the business into a modern, national and increasingly partnership-led operation, delivering strong results for sellers while giving estate agents a valuable additional route to market.”

Shaw also emphasised Gale’s expertise and ability to build trusted, long-term relationships. “Daniel combines considerable auction expertise with commercial focus and an ability to build trusted, long-term relationships. He thoroughly deserves this recognition and will play a central role as we continue to expand our auction services across LRG and through our growing network of independent partners.”

Gale commented on the evolving auction market, noting its growing appeal among sellers. “The auction market has changed significantly during my career and is increasingly being chosen as a first-choice route by sellers who value certainty, transparency and a defined timeframe,” he said. “We have built a service that allows agents to offer those benefits while retaining their relationship with the client, supported by our specialist team throughout the process.”

Looking ahead, Gale plans to focus on expanding the partnership model to more agents across the country, investing in the team and service, and continuing to deliver strong results for sellers. This promotion marks a new chapter for First for Auctions, as it seeks to solidify its position as a leading player in the UK auction market.

item.title: Property auction sales slide as market loses momentum
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property auction activity slowed in July, with fewer homes selling under the hammer compared to the previous month, according to the latest figures from Essential Information Group (EIG). The national success rate dipped to 64.7%, reflecting broader cooling trends across the UK housing market.

Auction Market Sees Decline in Sales and Revenue

The latest data reveals a 2.4% year-on-year drop in properties offered at auction, while the number of successful sales fell more sharply by 8.8%. The total value of properties sold also decreased significantly, with £540 million raised in July – down 18.6% from the same period last year. This mirrors Rightmove's findings showing a 6% annual decline in buyer demand during the same month.

Commercial property auctions proved more resilient, maintaining slightly higher transaction volumes than last year. However, residential auctions saw steeper declines, with 10.1% fewer lots sold compared to July 2025.

Regional Variations in Auction Performance

The slowdown hasn't been evenly distributed across the country. London and the South West showed the strongest growth between May and July, while Yorkshire and the Humber also outperformed last year's figures. Scotland continued its growth trajectory, albeit from a lower baseline.

Meanwhile, the East Midlands and North East experienced weaker sales volumes, with several regions also recording falls in the total value of properties sold at auction. These regional disparities highlight how local market conditions continue to influence auction outcomes.

Long-Term Outlook Remains Positive

Despite July's slowdown, EIG's managing director David Sandeman noted that the 12-month picture shows encouraging growth: "Lots offered and sold over the past year remain up 11.7% and 10.1% respectively."

Market observers typically expect a seasonal dip during the summer months, with activity traditionally picking up again in autumn. Those considering auction purchases may wish to monitor how these trends develop post-summer, particularly in their local areas.

As the market adjusts to current economic conditions, potential buyers and sellers might find auctions offer alternative opportunities, though professional advice remains crucial when navigating this specialist sector.

item.title: What happens to £750m of unclaimed tenancy deposits?
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

An estimated £750m in unclaimed or dormant tenancy deposits may be sitting within the deposit protection system in England and Wales, according to recent analysis by The Letting Partnership. This significant sum highlights a potential gap in the current framework, as there are no formal rules governing what happens to deposits when tenants fail to reclaim them after their tenancy ends. Whilst reforms have focused on how deposits should be protected in the future, less attention has been paid to addressing dormant funds.

The Current Framework

In England and Wales, tenancy deposits must be protected in a government-approved scheme, ensuring that funds are safeguarded for tenants. However, unlike other financial systems, there is no formal dormancy framework for these deposits. This means there are no clear rules defining when a deposit becomes dormant or what should happen to genuinely unclaimed funds. The Letting Partnership’s estimate of £750m is based on publicly available housing and tenancy deposit data, though no official consolidated figures currently exist.

The organisation has emphasised that this estimate does not imply wrongdoing by letting agents or deposit protection schemes. Instead, it highlights a gap in the existing system that could benefit from clearer governance. Without a formal framework, there is no official reporting mechanism to reconcile deposits held within protection schemes against those still active in letting agents’ portfolios. This leaves uncertainty for all parties involved, including tenants, landlords, and deposit protection providers.

Lessons from Scotland

Scotland operates a different system, where legislation allows eligible dormant tenancy deposits to support housing-related causes once specific safeguards and timeframes are met. This approach provides a clear pathway for handling unclaimed funds whilst ensuring they are used for public benefit. The Letting Partnership has called on policymakers in England and Wales to consider adopting a similar framework as part of wider tenancy deposit reforms.

Such a system could offer greater clarity and certainty for all stakeholders. For tenants, it would establish clear rules for reclaiming deposits, whilst landlords and letting agents would benefit from a defined process for handling dormant funds. Deposit protection providers would also gain a structured approach to managing unclaimed deposits, potentially reducing administrative burdens.

The Need for Better Data

Before implementing any changes, The Letting Partnership has stressed the importance of gathering better data on dormant deposits. Currently, there is no comprehensive picture of how many deposits remain unclaimed after tenancies end. Improved data collection and reporting mechanisms could help policymakers make more informed decisions and ensure any reforms are effective and fair.

Chris Mason, COO of The Letting Partnership, commented: “The tenancy deposit reform debate has understandably focused on how deposits should be protected in the future, but there is a wider governance question that also deserves attention. At present, there is no legislative framework in England and Wales governing dormant tenancy deposits, nor is there any official reporting mechanism that reconciles deposits held within the protection schemes against those that remain active within letting agents’ portfolios.”

As discussions around tenancy deposit reform continue, addressing the issue of dormant deposits could provide an opportunity to create a more robust and transparent system. Borrowers, landlords, and tenants alike may benefit from clearer rules and a framework that ensures unclaimed funds are handled appropriately.

item.title: Market holding ‘broadly stable’ in latest HPI
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The housing market continues to show resilience, with recent data suggesting stability despite ongoing economic challenges. According to the latest House Price Index (HPI), property values remain broadly steady, offering a sense of reassurance for both buyers and sellers. Industry experts anticipate that market activity could strengthen in the coming months, driven by improving affordability and more settled borrowing costs.

Factors Contributing to Market Stability

Several elements are playing a role in maintaining the current balance within the property market. Mortgage rates, which saw significant fluctuations in recent years, appear to be stabilising, providing borrowers with greater certainty. Additionally, wage growth and softer house price rises are helping to ease affordability pressures, making homeownership more attainable for many.

Economists also point to the Bank of England’s decision to hold the base rate steady as a positive factor. This pause in rate hikes has allowed lenders to offer more competitive mortgage deals, encouraging potential buyers to enter the market. While inflation remains a concern, its gradual decline is expected to further support housing demand.

What Could Drive Future Growth?

Looking ahead, experts suggest that a combination of factors could stimulate increased activity in the property market. Improved consumer confidence, coupled with stable interest rates, may encourage more homeowners to consider moving or investing in property. First-time buyers, in particular, could benefit from government schemes and lender incentives designed to make mortgages more accessible.

Regional variations are also expected to play a role, with some areas likely to see stronger growth than others. Cities with robust employment opportunities and infrastructure developments are predicted to attract higher levels of buyer interest. Meanwhile, the rental market remains competitive, potentially prompting more tenants to explore homeownership as a long-term solution.

What Should Borrowers Consider?

For those planning to enter the property market, it could be worth reviewing their financial position carefully. Comparing mortgage deals from different lenders may help secure favourable terms, whilst seeking independent advice could provide clarity on the options available. Homeowners considering remortgaging might also find opportunities to reduce their monthly payments or lock in a fixed rate for added security.

Whilst the market appears stable, external factors such as geopolitical events or changes in economic policy could influence future trends. Staying informed and prepared for potential shifts is advisable for anyone navigating the property landscape.

In summary, the housing market’s current stability offers a promising outlook for buyers and sellers alike. With affordability improving and borrowing costs settling, the coming months could see a gradual uptick in activity, supported by a mix of economic and regional factors.

item.title: PM’s regeneration plans succeed or fail on private investment
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The success of the government's ambitious regeneration plans may hinge on the ability to attract substantial private investment, according to property market experts. With significant infrastructure and housing projects proposed across the UK, policymakers face the challenge of creating conditions that appeal to institutional investors and developers alike.

Private sector crucial for large-scale regeneration

Urban regeneration projects typically require billions in funding that simply cannot be met by public finances alone. Industry analysts suggest that for the government's vision to become reality, local authorities and development agencies will need to work closely with private investors to bridge the funding gap. These partnerships could take various forms, from joint ventures to carefully structured investment frameworks.

Property specialists highlight several factors that influence private investment decisions in regeneration schemes. These include clear planning processes, stable political environments, and realistic timelines for project completion. Where these elements align, private capital has historically followed - as seen in successful transformations of areas like London's King's Cross and Manchester's Northern Quarter.

Balancing public benefit with investor returns

One of the key challenges for policymakers lies in creating regeneration models that deliver community benefits while still providing acceptable returns for private investors. Mixed-use developments that combine residential, commercial and leisure spaces often present the most viable solutions. Such projects can revitalise local economies while offering investors diversified revenue streams.

Industry observers note that tax incentives and streamlined planning procedures could play important roles in attracting private capital. The government's proposed investment zones, with their promised tax reliefs and planning simplifications, may provide useful test cases for this approach. However, critics caution that any incentives must be carefully designed to avoid unintended consequences in local housing markets.

For homeowners and prospective buyers, successful regeneration can bring both opportunities and challenges. While improved infrastructure and amenities typically boost property values, there may be short-term disruption during construction phases. Those considering property purchases in regeneration areas might wish to research planned developments thoroughly before committing.

item.title: HMO landlords plan £10,000 improvement spend
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords operating houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) are reportedly planning to invest significantly in property improvements, with many budgeting up to £10,000 per property. This comes as rental yields remain robust, encouraging property owners to enhance the quality, compliance, and energy efficiency of their investments.

Focus on Property Quality and Compliance

HMO landlords are increasingly prioritising property quality and compliance with regulations. With stricter rules governing rental properties, particularly HMOs, landlords are focusing on ensuring their properties meet all legal requirements. This includes upgrading safety features, improving living conditions, and maintaining high standards of accommodation. Such investments not only help avoid potential penalties but also make properties more attractive to tenants, potentially reducing void periods.

Energy Efficiency Upgrades

Another key area of spending is energy efficiency. With rising energy costs and growing tenant demand for sustainable living spaces, landlords are investing in upgrades such as double glazing, insulation, and energy-efficient heating systems. These improvements can lead to lower utility bills for tenants, making the property more appealing. Additionally, energy-efficient properties may benefit from higher rental values and improved long-term asset value.

Strong Rental Returns Drive Investment

The decision to invest in property improvements is bolstered by the strong rental returns currently seen in the HMO market. Despite economic uncertainties, demand for shared accommodation remains high, particularly in urban areas where affordability is a concern for many tenants. This steady demand provides landlords with the confidence to reinvest in their properties, ensuring they remain competitive in the market.

For landlords considering upgrades, it could be worth exploring financing options tailored to property improvements. Ensuring properties meet modern standards not only benefits tenants but can also enhance the overall profitability of HMO investments.

item.title: Estate agents escape blame as almost three-quarters of home movers face delays
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent research reveals that 72% of UK home movers faced delays during their property transactions, yet estate agents largely escaped blame for these hold-ups. The average home move now takes 216 days from listing to completion – 36 days longer than in 2019 according to Rightmove data. While the property industry acknowledges these challenges, professionals remain divided on potential solutions.

Where delays occur – and who bears the blame

The home-moving process has become notably slower, with sellers typically waiting 62 days to secure a buyer before facing a further 154-day journey to completion. When delayed movers identified responsibility, half pointed to conveyancers or solicitors, while 40% attributed delays to the other party in the transaction. Only 5% held estate agents accountable.

Regional variations paint a striking picture, with Londoners (80%), East Midlands residents (79%), and movers in Wales and the North West (78%) reporting the highest delay rates. Scotland fared considerably better at 43%, suggesting different market dynamics or legal processes may influence transaction speeds.

Industry divided on solutions

Property professionals show little consensus on how to streamline transactions. Estate agents predominantly advocate for:

  • Faster communication (33%)
  • Shared case tracking (25%)
  • Integrated digital systems (10%)

Conveyancers take a different view, prioritising:

  • Better understanding between professions (23%)
  • Clearer client expectations (21%)
  • Only 13% see faster communication as the primary solution

Mortgage brokers balanced their preferences equally between improved communication and agreed service standards (22% each), while nearly 30% of surveyors doubted any proposed measures would significantly enhance working relationships.

Professional relationships under scrutiny

The research uncovered notable disparities in how property professionals perceive their working relationships. Estate agents appear more positive about their collaborations, with 67% describing relationships with conveyancers as good – a sentiment only reciprocated by 50% of conveyancers. Similar gaps exist between agents and surveyors (54% versus 44%) and in mortgage advice relationships (58% of agents versus 54% of brokers holding positive views).

These findings suggest that while the industry recognises transaction delays as problematic, solutions may require more coordinated efforts between different professional groups. Homeowners embarking on a move might benefit from understanding these potential friction points when planning their property journey.

item.title: Estate agents face September slowdown as viewings take a hit
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The start of the autumn property market could see a slowdown, with many parents of school-aged children expecting their house-hunting activities to take a backseat as family routines resume. According to recent research by House Buyer Bureau, nearly nine in ten (88%) parents anticipate booking or attending fewer property viewings during the first few weeks of the new school term. This trend could have a ripple effect on the broader property market, as buyers juggle childcare and other commitments.

Family Commitments Impact Property Searches

For parents, the return to school often means a shift in priorities. The study found that 86% of respondents expect to spend less time actively searching for a new home, with childcare responsibilities cited as the biggest obstacle by 24% of parents. Other challenges include school drop-offs and pick-ups (22%), after-school clubs and activities (13%), and the general demands of returning to work and re-establishing family routines (11%). As a result, estate agents may need to adapt their strategies to accommodate these changing schedules. For instance, 37% of parents prefer viewings during school hours, while 35% favour weekends. Evenings are the preferred time for 20%, with just 8% opting for after-school appointments.

Increased Reliance on Digital Tools

With buyers having less time for in-person viewings, digital marketing tools are likely to play a more prominent role in the property market. Nearly four in five (79%) parents expect to rely more heavily on online listings, virtual tours, or video viewings when searching for their next home. This shift towards digital solutions could help estate agents maintain engagement with buyers during this period of reduced activity.

However, the slowdown may not be limited to viewings alone. The research also highlights potential delays in sales progression, with 92% of respondents stating that school commitments could slow their purchase process. Tasks such as dealing with paperwork, attending mortgage appointments, and managing surveys may prove more challenging amidst busy family schedules. Three-quarters of parents believe it could take more than a month before they can fully focus on their property search again, with just 12% expecting to return to normal activity within a week.

Longer-Term Effects on the Market

Chris Hodgkinson, managing director of House Buyer Bureau, noted that the impact of school commitments on the property market may extend beyond the initial weeks of September. He explained, “Traditionally, September marks the point at which the property market starts to regain momentum after the summer holidays. However, for parents, the return to school can leave little time for searching for a home, attending viewings, or progressing a purchase. This may not be a short-lived blip, as many parents believe it could take over a month before they can fully re-engage with the market.”

Estate agents and sellers may need to exercise patience during this period, as buyers navigate the demands of the school year. Flexibility in scheduling and a greater emphasis on digital tools could help bridge the gap, ensuring that interest in properties remains steady even as physical viewings decline.

item.title: Renters’ Rights Act piles more work on letting agents
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The Renters’ Rights Act, introduced on 1 May, has significantly impacted the workload of letting agents across the UK. According to recent research by Propoly, 73% of property professionals report an increase in administrative tasks since the legislation came into force. For a quarter of respondents, the effect on their business has been particularly pronounced, with compliance and record-keeping emerging as the primary sources of additional work.

Increased Administrative Demands

One of the key challenges identified by letting agents is the heightened administrative burden. Compliance and record-keeping were cited by 18% of respondents as the most time-consuming tasks, followed by rent reviews (16%) and managing possessions and tenancy endings (14%). The Act has also necessitated closer collaboration between lettings and property management teams, with half of respondents noting that staff now need to work more cohesively.

Technology, while often seen as a solution to streamline processes, appears to be adding to the complexity for some agents. Only 17% of businesses use a single, integrated system to manage the additional work created by the Renters’ Rights Act. Two-thirds rely on multiple disconnected systems, and another 17% depend heavily on emails, spreadsheets, and other manual processes. This fragmentation can lead to inefficiencies, with 61% of respondents reporting that staff often have to transfer, re-enter, or duplicate information across different platforms.

The Need for Better Integration

The lack of integration between systems is a significant issue for many letting agents. More than half (52%) believe that better links between their systems would improve efficiency. Landlord communication and decision-making were identified as areas that could benefit most from improved integration, followed by tenant referencing, compliance, and tenant communications.

Sim Sekhon, group chief executive officer at Propoly, commented: “Over 100 days since the introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act, it’s clear that the impact extends beyond just additional work. Lettings businesses now need to rethink how they organise their people, processes, and technology to ensure information flows efficiently between teams and systems involved in managing a tenancy.”

Ongoing Compliance Challenges

Compliance remains a major concern for letting agents, with 28% of respondents expecting it to become their biggest operational challenge under the Renters’ Rights Act. Maintaining profitability whilst managing the additional workload was flagged by 21% of respondents, while 16% pointed to the overall administrative burden as a key issue.

As the sector continues to adapt to these changes, the focus will likely remain on finding ways to streamline processes and improve efficiency. For many agents, investing in better technology and fostering closer collaboration between teams could be essential steps in navigating the challenges posed by the Renters’ Rights Act.

With the legislation still in its early stages, it remains to be seen how letting agents will continue to evolve their practices to meet these new demands. However, one thing is clear: the Renters’ Rights Act has ushered in a period of significant change for the industry.

item.title: Renters’ Rights Act drives landlords towards greater use of guarantors
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Landlords are increasingly turning to guarantor requests for tenants following recent changes under the Renters’ Rights Act, according to new research. With the legislation now preventing landlords from asking for more than one month’s rent upfront, many are tightening their income checks and seeking alternative safeguards – potentially creating challenges for renters without access to guarantors.

Guarantor requests on the rise

The Summer 2026 Lettings Report surveyed over 1,500 landlords and tenants across England and Wales, revealing that 54% of landlords now more frequently request guarantors when prospective tenants fail standard affordability checks. This shift comes as the Renters’ Rights Act removes the option for landlords to request multiple months’ rent in advance as security.

Among tenants without personal guarantors, the research found:

  • 51% would seek cheaper accommodation
  • 16% would pause their property search entirely
  • Only 18% would consider paid guarantor services

Awareness of commercial guarantor services remains strikingly low, with 74% of tenants completely unfamiliar with the concept and just 2% having ever used such services. Separate research indicates 34% of renters didn’t understand what a guarantor was when first asked to provide one.

Alternative protections gaining traction

Whilst 28% of landlords reported no change in their guarantor policies and 13% maintained existing practices, some are exploring different risk-management solutions. Rent guarantee insurance appears to be growing in popularity, with 37% of landlords already holding policies and a further 19% considering coverage. However, 17% remained unaware such products existed.

The English Housing Survey 2024-25 found that 20% of private renters already required guarantors before the legislative changes, suggesting the practice was already widespread in certain market segments. Industry experts suggest that clearer communication about tenant verification options may benefit both landlords and renters navigating the new regulatory environment.

Allison Thompson of LRG noted: “Landlords need confidence in a tenancy’s affordability, particularly now that advance rent payments are no longer available as an additional safeguard.” The findings highlight how regulatory changes can unintentionally reshape rental market dynamics, with implications for housing accessibility.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Two leading UK property consultancies have announced high-profile appointments this month, signalling continued confidence in the specialist rural and commercial property sectors. Knight Frank has named a new head for its national country department, while BTG Eddisons has expanded its North West team with an experienced commercial property director.

Knight Frank appoints new country property head

Will Matthews, known professionally as "Stan", has taken over as head of Knight Frank's national country department following Edward Rook's decade-long tenure. The London-based team handles premium country properties, averaging over £400m in annual sales during Rook's leadership.

Matthews brings two decades of experience at Knight Frank to the role, having joined in 2003. He initially specialised in prime country house sales before moving into farms and estates. Since 2022, he has led the firm's Farms and Estates team while advising on rural property transactions nationwide.

Rook commented: "Will understands every aspect of the country market. The department will continue to thrive under his leadership." Despite current market challenges, the team completed £173m of prime country house sales in early 2026.

Matthews noted the enduring demand for specialist rural property advice, stating: "Our clients continue to seek expertise across country houses, farms and estates. We look forward to building on our success."

Commercial property veteran joins BTG Eddisons

Meanwhile, commercial property consultancy BTG Eddisons has strengthened its North West operations with the appointment of Ian Steele as director. Steele joins after seven years as principal at Avison Young's Liverpool office, bringing over 30 years' experience in the North West commercial property market.

Steele will focus on office agency and development markets across Liverpool and Manchester, working alongside directors Robert Diggle and David Baker. His appointment reflects growing demand for commercial property expertise in the region.

Luke Tillison, BTG Eddisons' head of transactional, said: "Ian is well established in the Liverpool market with an exceptional network. His expertise will prove invaluable as we expand our regional services."

These strategic appointments suggest both firms remain optimistic about long-term prospects in their respective property sectors, despite current economic uncertainties. Homeowners and investors may wish to monitor how these leadership changes affect market dynamics in coming months.
